passage: Public discussion tends to treat time alone as a problem to be solved. Loneliness is described, rightly, as a source of real suffering, and the remedies proposed, from neighbourhood programmes to ever more ingenious ways of connecting online, share an assumption: that the less time a person spends unaccompanied, the better. On this view solitude and loneliness are a single condition seen from two angles, the first merely a polite name for the second.

The assumption confuses a fact about circumstances with a fact about experience. Loneliness is the painful sense that one's connections are fewer or thinner than one needs; it can be felt in a crowded room, and some of its most persistent forms occur within marriages and among colleagues who see each other every day. Solitude is simply being alone, and its quality depends on what one brings to it. For someone who is lonely, an empty evening confirms a lack. For someone who is not, the same evening may be the only time in the week when attention is not divided, when a thought can be followed to its end, or when grief or pleasure can be felt without being performed for anyone.

Many traditions have valued this second kind of aloneness. Hermits, monks and contemplatives have sought it deliberately, sometimes for years at a time, and periods of withdrawal into wilderness or retreat recur in the stories told about religious teachers in very different cultures. One need not share their aims to see the point they grasped: a person who can never bear his own company depends on others in a way that makes his relationships less free. Friendship is richer between people who could survive without it.

This is not an argument for withdrawal. Solitude is good largely because it is chosen and because it comes to an end; a solitude imposed by exclusion, or one that stretches on with no prospect of return, turns into the very loneliness from which it was supposed to be distinct. Nor is the capacity to be alone a substitute for company; it is a companion skill to it. But if the two conditions really are distinct, then policies and technologies that aim only at reducing time spent alone may, without anyone intending it, crowd out a good that most people need in some measure and few are ever taught to use. The cure for loneliness is better connection, not the abolition of solitude.

passage: The sterile worker castes of ants, bees and wasps troubled Darwin as much as almost any feature of the living world. A creature that never reproduces cannot pass on whatever traits make it a good worker, so it was hard to see how natural selection could have refined the elaborate behaviour of workers over many generations. Darwin's tentative answer was that selection might act on the family rather than on the individual, much as a breeder who wants a good strain of cattle keeps the relatives of an animal whose worth became clear only after it was slaughtered.

The idea was given a precise form only in the twentieth century. A gene that disposes its bearer to help relatives can spread even if the bearer leaves no offspring of its own, provided the help raises the reproduction of relatives who are likely to carry copies of the same gene. What matters is the product of two quantities, the benefit to the relative and the probability that the relative shares the gene, weighed against the cost to the helper. Sterility, on this account, is not an anomaly to be explained away but an extreme point on a continuum of helping, reached when a helper can do more for its genes by raising siblings than by raising young of its own.

For a time, a further detail seemed to make the case almost too neat. In ants, bees and wasps, males develop from unfertilised eggs, and a peculiarity of inheritance follows: sisters who share both parents are, on average, more closely related to one another than a mother is to her daughters. If workers are more closely related to their sisters than to their own potential offspring, raising sisters is the better genetic bargain, and sterile castes should arise readily in exactly these insects. The argument was elegant, and it was widely taught. It has not survived well. Termites, whose inheritance has no such peculiarity, have sterile castes too; the queens of many ants and bees mate with several males, which dilutes the relatedness among their daughters; and the great majority of species with this peculiar inheritance are not social at all.

The lesson is not that kinship is irrelevant. Workers in social insect colonies typically do raise relatives, and the general principle remains the best account of why they can afford to forgo reproduction. The lesson is rather that relatedness is only one term in the calculation. Ecological conditions that make independent breeding hopeless, such as a scarce nest site that must be defended or food that only a group can gather, raise the benefit of helping and can tip the balance even where relatedness is modest. The special feature of inheritance made a good story, but the more durable explanation lies in the interaction of kinship with circumstance.

passage: Insurance works by pooling: many people each pay a modest premium so that the few who suffer a loss can be compensated, and the arrangement rests on a fact that is easy to overlook: no one in the pool knows in advance who the unlucky will be. If the pool holds a mixture of people whose risks differ but cannot be told apart, a single price can cover everyone, and the careful and the careless alike buy protection they value.

The trouble begins when buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer does. Those who expect to claim find a uniform premium a bargain; those who expect not to find it expensive, and some of them leave. The insurer, seeing claims rise relative to premiums, raises the price, which drives out the next group of relatively safe customers. In the extreme case the pool shrinks until only the riskiest remain, and a product that many people would have wanted cannot be sold at a price that anyone else will pay. Economists call this unravelling adverse selection, and it can happen even though no one has lied to anyone.

Two remedies are available, and neither is free. The first is for insurers to close the gap in information through medical examinations, questionnaires and records of past claims. Each of these helps, yet each also wears away the pooling that made insurance worth having, because a pool sorted precisely by risk is no longer sharing much risk at all. A person found to have a costly condition before buying cover will be quoted a premium close to the expected cost of treating it, which is to say no insurance in any useful sense. The second remedy is to make membership compulsory or nearly universal, so that the low-risk cannot walk away. This keeps the pool mixed, but it asks the healthy to subsidise the sick on terms that some of them did not choose and regard as unfair.

The choice between these remedies is often presented as a technical matter for actuaries, but it is better understood as a choice about how much of life's bad luck a society wishes to share. For risks that people largely take on by choice, such as a dangerous hobby, pricing by risk seems fair enough. For risks that arrive at birth or by pure chance, sorting begins to look like penalising people twice: once through fate, and again through the price.

passage: The ordinary picture of pain is that of a gauge. Tissue is damaged, nerves carry a report of the damage to the brain, and the strength of the pain reflects the size of the injury, much as the needle on a dial reflects the pressure in a pipe. The picture is intuitive and, for a great many everyday injuries, roughly accurate. A burnt finger hurts more than a scratched one, and both stop hurting as they heal.

The difficulty is that the gauge picture fails precisely where pain matters most. People sometimes suffer serious wounds in moments of danger or intense concentration and feel little until the moment has passed. Others feel vivid pain in limbs that have been amputated, where there is no tissue left to report anything. Most troubling of all, a large number of people continue to hurt for months or years after an injury has, by every available measure, healed. If pain were a reading of damage, none of this should happen. A pressure gauge that behaved in these ways would simply be sent back for repair.

An alternative account treats pain not as a reading but as a verdict. Signals from the tissues are one input among several; the brain combines them with context, expectation and memory, and produces pain when it concludes that the body is under threat and needs protecting. On this account, the soldier who feels nothing has a brain occupied with a greater threat, the amputee's brain is responding to a map of a body part that persists after the part is gone, and long-lasting pain may reflect a protective system that has grown oversensitive, raising the alarm long after the danger has passed.

This account is sometimes heard as a polite way of saying that the pain is imaginary, and patients with long-standing pain have good reason to be wary of anything that sounds like that. But the claim is the reverse. A verdict produced by the nervous system is as real as any other bodily event, and it hurts just as much. What changes is where treatment might be aimed. If the alarm itself has become oversensitive, then searching ever harder for a damaged structure, and operating on whatever turns up in a scan, may do little good, while approaches that address the protective system as a whole, through explanation, graded activity and attention to fear, may help where repairs to the tissues did not.

passage: When a trait is described as highly heritable, many readers hear a claim about destiny: if height or some aspect of temperament is 'mostly genetic', then upbringing can do little to alter it. The inference feels natural, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what heritability measures. Heritability is a statistic about a population, not about a person. It estimates what share of the variation in a trait, across a particular group living in a particular range of environments, can be statistically associated with genetic differences among the members of that group. It says nothing about how much of any one individual's height was produced by genes, a question that is not even coherent, since every centimetre of a person's height required both genes and food.

Two consequences follow, and both tend to surprise people. First, heritability depends on the environment in which it is measured. If every child in a group were given exactly the same diet, schooling and care, the remaining differences among them would be largely genetic, and the heritability of almost any trait would rise, not because genes had become more powerful but because the environmental differences had been taken away. Conversely, in a group where some children are well fed and others go hungry, differences in nutrition will account for much of the variation in height, and the measured heritability will fall. Second, a trait can be built almost entirely by genes and still show low heritability. Nearly everyone is born with five fingers on each hand because a developmental programme laid down in the genome builds them; most people who have fewer have lost them through injury. Variation in finger number is therefore mainly environmental, even though the fingers themselves are anything but.

The most consequential error concerns differences between groups. Suppose a trait is highly heritable within each of two populations. It is tempting to conclude that the average difference between the populations must also be largely genetic. It need not be. Picture two handfuls of seed taken from the same genetically varied sack, one sown in rich soil and the other in poor soil. Within each plot, differences in height will be largely genetic, since the soil is uniform; between the plots, the difference is due entirely to the soil. High heritability within groups is compatible with a gap between them that has no genetic basis at all.

None of this makes heritability useless. Breeders rely on it to predict how quickly a herd will respond to selection, and researchers use it to judge where genetic studies are likely to find something. The fault lies not with the statistic but with the habit of reading it as a measure of fixity. A highly heritable trait may still be changed by changing the environment; short sight is substantially heritable, and spectacles correct it all the same.

passage: The maxim that there is no disputing about taste is usually offered as a courtesy. When two people disagree about a film or a piece of music, one of them, sensing that the conversation is about to turn sour, observes that it is all a matter of taste, and the other, relieved, agrees. The maxim seems to express a modern and admirable humility, for who is anyone to tell another person what to enjoy? But the courtesy rests on a confusion, and the confusion has consequences for the way we talk about art and, in the end, for the way we treat one another.

The confusion is between preference and judgement. If you dislike the taste of coriander and I like it, there is nothing for us to argue about. Neither of us thinks the other has missed something; we simply report different reactions, and the reports do not compete, any more than your being cold and my being warm in the same room amounts to a disagreement about the room. Disagreements about novels or buildings are rarely like this. When I say that a novel is sentimental and you say that it is moving, each of us means to be saying something about the book, and each of us expects the other to be able, at least in principle, to recognise it. We point to passages, compare the novel with others, and draw attention to what the other may have overlooked. These are the moves of people who believe there is something to be right about, even if neither of them can prove it.

The relativist replies that this behaviour, however common, rests on an illusion. There is no fact about the book's sentimentality independent of readers' reactions, the argument runs, and so our disputes, unlike disputes about the boiling point of water, can never be settled; at most one party tires and gives up. This reply assumes that a dispute is worth having only if it can end in proof. Aesthetic argument, however, does not aim at proof. It aims at a change in perception, and its success is the moment when you look again at the passage I have pointed to and hear the false note I heard, or when I, rereading it at your insistence, find that what I took for manipulation is in fact restraint. Such moments are not rare. Most people can remember a friend, a teacher or a critic who showed them something they had not been able to see, and they do not remember the experience as having been talked into a preference; they remember it as having learned something.

It must be granted that some disagreements reach a floor. Two careful readers may agree about every feature of a poem, its rhythm, its imagery, its debts and its departures, and still differ about whether it is good, because one prizes austerity and the other abundance. At this point argument may genuinely run out, and it is sensible to say so. But the floor lies far lower than the maxim implies. Most disputes about taste break off long before they reach it, not because the parties have exhausted their reasons, but because one of them has invoked the maxim in order to end the conversation.

There is, finally, something less humble in the maxim than it appears. To tell someone that their view of a novel is merely a matter of taste is to decline to treat it as a view at all, that is, as a claim that might be true and from which one might learn. The maxim protects both parties from the risk of being wrong, but it does so at the price of the possibility of being changed. Real respect for another person's judgement would consist in disputing it.

passage: Debates about the origin of life have long been organised around a chicken-and-egg problem. In every living cell today, the information needed to build proteins is stored in nucleic acids, while the work of copying those nucleic acids is done by proteins. Neither seems able to arise without the other. One family of proposals breaks the circle by giving priority to the molecule that carries information: life began, on this view, when some molecule capable of copying itself appeared, however clumsily, and natural selection among its variants did the rest. A rival family gives priority to chemistry that sustains itself: life began as networks of reactions, perhaps on mineral surfaces near hot springs on the sea floor, that captured energy from their surroundings and kept themselves going long before any of their components stored heritable information.

The case for putting the replicator first gained great force from a discovery about RNA, a close chemical relative of DNA. RNA, it turned out, can not only carry information but also catalyse reactions, and the core of the machinery that assembles proteins in every cell is itself made of RNA. A world in which RNA did both jobs, storing instructions and doing chemical work, would dissolve the chicken-and-egg problem, and that protein-building machinery looks very much like a relic of such a world. Replicator theorists add a deeper argument. Without heredity, they say, there is no evolution in any serious sense: a chemical network that merely persists cannot accumulate improvements, because there is nothing to record which variants did better.

Metabolism-first theorists reply that the RNA world has a chemistry problem it has never solved. The building blocks of RNA are intricate molecules, hard to make without the help of enzymes and prone to fall apart in water; assembling them into long chains that can copy themselves requires a degree of order that seems unlikely to arise unaided. Self-sustaining reaction networks, by contrast, need only simple ingredients and a source of energy. These theorists also argue that heredity need not wait for a dedicated molecule. A network in which certain reactions reinforce one another could persist in several alternative states, and if fragments that break away from a network tend to restart the same state, something like inheritance exists before any gene.

It is worth noticing that the two camps are often answering different questions. Replicator theorists ask what made open-ended evolution possible, and their answer, a molecule that copies information with modest accuracy, is hard to dispute as an account of that threshold. Metabolism theorists ask where the materials and energy for any such molecule came from, and their answer, a geochemical setting that drives reactions without the help of life, is equally hard to dispute as an account of the prior stage. Presented as rivals, each side scores easy points against the other's weakest claim: that replicators could assemble themselves in a chemical vacuum, or that self-maintaining networks could evolve indefinitely without anything like genes.

The more promising view, then, treats the problem as one of sequence rather than of priority in the abstract. A chemistry able to sustain itself may have been the setting in which the first replicators formed and on which they depended, and the replicators may in turn have captured and refined the network that fed them. This does not settle the matter, since the details of each stage remain obscure and may never be recovered from a planet whose earliest rocks have been largely destroyed. But it changes what counts as progress. The question is no longer which came first, as though one of them had to be the true beginning, but how a world of self-maintaining chemistry could have given rise to one in which information was inherited.

passage: Labour law in most countries rests on a binary. A worker is either an employee, who accepts direction in exchange for a wage and a bundle of protections, or an independent contractor, who sells a result, chooses her own methods and bears her own risks. The line was drawn for a world in which the difference was usually obvious: the clerk at a desk was one, the plumber who came to fix the office pipes was the other. Platform work has made the line hard to find. A driver who logs into an app chooses when to work and may refuse any job, which looks like independence; the same driver cannot set the fare, does not know which passenger comes next, and can be removed by an algorithm whose criteria she never sees, which looks very much like direction.

Two responses dominate the debate. One holds that platform workers are employees in all but name and that courts should simply say so. The other holds that flexibility is the whole attraction of such work, that many who do it also study or hold other jobs, and that imposing fixed shifts, minimum hours and the rest of the employment bundle would destroy the thing they value. Each side is right about what the other ignores. The first is right that the platform exercises a control over the terms of work that no genuine contractor would accept; the second is right that the employment bundle was designed around a fixed schedule and a single employer, and fits awkwardly onto someone who works eleven hours one week for three different apps and none the next.

What both share is the assumption that protections must come as a package attached to a status. That assumption is a historical accident rather than a principle. Some protections, such as a minimum rate for time actually worked, insurance against injury on the job or a right to be told why an account was suspended, depend on nothing that a flexible schedule makes impossible. Others, such as paid holidays calculated over a working year, are harder to translate, though not obviously impossible if entitlements accrue by the hour and follow the worker rather than the firm.

Unbundling has dangers of its own. A menu of separable protections invites firms to lobby for the cheapest selection, and a third category of worker, introduced to accommodate the platforms, could become a convenient place to move people who are at present employees. The case for unbundling is therefore not that it is free of risk, but that the binary has already failed: forcing a new form of work into one of two old boxes guarantees that, whichever box is chosen, a large part of the reality will be misdescribed.

passage: Arguments about the literary canon are usually conducted as arguments about a list. One side defends a set of books as the best that a tradition has produced; the other replies that the list was drawn up by a narrow group of readers and reflects their tastes and their blind spots. Both sides, for all their hostility, agree on what a canon is: a ranking, a roll of honour, a verdict on quality that can be revised by adding names or striking them out. It is worth asking whether that shared assumption is right.

A different account fits the actual history of canons better. On this account a work becomes canonical not because readers judge it excellent but because later writers cannot leave it alone. They answer it, parody it, borrow its situations, quarrel with its conclusions and rewrite it from the point of view of a character it neglected. The canonical work is then the one you must have read in order to understand a great many others; its status is less a medal than a position in a network of replies. This explains something the list model cannot. Canons contain works that almost everyone agrees are clumsy, uneven or dull in long stretches, and they exclude works of great finish that simply provoked no answer. A ranking by quality would not look like that; a record of a conversation would.

The account has a consequence for those who wish to change the canon. If canonical status is conferred by later writing rather than by verdict, then a syllabus committee cannot make a book canonical by placing it on a reading list, any more than a critic could remove one by declaring it overrated. What can be done is to put neglected works where future writers will meet them, in print, in translation and in the classroom, and then to wait and see whether they are taken up.

Yet the conversational canon is not thereby cleared of the exclusions its critics describe. Who gets to join a conversation depends on who was taught to read, who could find a publisher and whose replies were preserved. A tradition in which most writers came from one class or one sex will have conducted its conversation largely among them, and the canon it produced will reflect that. The conversational account does not answer the critics of the canon; it relocates their complaint, from the judgements of tastemakers to the conditions under which people could write at all, and that is where the remedy, if there is one, must be sought.

passage: Any science of consciousness faces an awkward fact at its foundation. The thing it studies is, by most accounts, directly available only to the person who has it, and the scientist learns about it chiefly through what that person says or otherwise signals: I saw the flash, or I did not; the face looked angry; the tone seemed to come from the left. Two opposite attitudes to this fact have been common. One holds that reports are so unreliable, so shaped by expectation, vocabulary and the wish to please, that a science resting on them is no science at all. The other treats a sincere report as the last word, since no one, it is said, is better placed than the subject to know what she experiences.

Neither attitude survives inspection, and the second is the easier to dismiss. People are often wrong about their own experience in ways that can be demonstrated: they confidently describe detail at the edges of their visual field that is not available to them, and they misjudge the order or timing of events they claim to have perceived. A report is a response produced by the subject, shaped by the question asked and the categories available, and it can misdescribe the experience it is about. But the first attitude draws the wrong conclusion from this. Every scientific instrument can misreport what it measures; the usual response is to study its errors, not to throw it away. A report is best treated as evidence about experience, fallible but informative, to be calibrated against other evidence rather than either revered or ignored.

The most productive methods have used reports in exactly this spirit. In masking experiments, the same image is shown on many trials, sometimes followed so quickly by a second image that the first is not reported as seen. Because the physical stimulus is held constant, differences in brain activity between seen and unseen trials can be attributed, at least tentatively, to the difference in experience rather than to the stimulus. The approach is powerful, but it carries a hidden complication. On seen trials the subject not only experiences the image but also prepares and makes a report about it, so some of the activity that distinguishes the two kinds of trial may belong to reporting rather than to experiencing.

To get around this, researchers have designed experiments in which subjects make no report at all, and conscious states are inferred from other signs, such as involuntary eye movements that track which of two competing images is being experienced. Critics point out a circle here: those signs were themselves validated by showing that they agree with reports. If reports are suspect, so, it seems, are the signs that stand in for them. The objection is clever, but it proves less than it appears to. The history of measurement is full of such circles. Early thermometers were checked against the sensation of warmth and then against one another, and in time they came to correct the very sensations against which they had first been checked. A circle of mutual calibration is vicious only if it never widens; when independent methods, each imperfect, are tested against one another and turn out to agree, confidence in all of them can rise together.

None of this guarantees that a science of consciousness will answer every question asked of it, and some philosophers doubt that any amount of correlating brain activity with reports could explain why experience exists at all. That doubt may be justified. But it is a doubt about the reach of the science, not about whether reports can serve as its data, and running the two together has done more to obscure the field than either the sceptics or the enthusiasts have usually admitted.

passage: The picture of the ageing mind that most people carry is one of steady decline. Memory falters, thinking slows, and the sharpness of youth gives way, from some point in early adulthood, to a long and gentle slide. The picture is not invented. On tasks that require rapid processing of unfamiliar information, such as spotting a target among distractors or holding several new items in mind while manipulating them, performance does fall with age, and the fall can be detected well before what anyone would call old age. But the picture has been assembled in a way that makes the decline look both steeper and more uniform than it is.

Much of the early evidence came from comparing people of different ages at a single moment, a method that is quick and cheap and was therefore used widely. A group of seventy-year-olds tested alongside a group of twenty-five-year-olds differs from it in more than age: the older group grew up with less schooling, different work and less familiarity with the kind of test being given. Studies that follow the same people over decades tend to show later and gentler declines than such snapshots suggest, though they carry biases of their own, since those who stay in a long study are often healthier and more able than those who drop out. Neither method gives a clean view, and the honest summary is that some decline is real, while its timing and size are less certain than the familiar picture implies.

More important, the familiar picture attends to only half of what changes. Knowledge of words, of facts, of how things usually go and how people usually behave, goes on accumulating well into later life, and on tests that draw on it older adults often outperform younger ones. Some researchers have gone further, proposing that part of the measured slowing reflects not failing machinery but a larger store: a mind that knows more words takes longer to find any one of them, much as a large library takes longer to search than a small one. The proposal is contested, and it cannot explain away every loss. It does, however, show that the same observation, a slower response, can be read as a symptom of deterioration or as a cost of accumulation, depending on what one assumes about the mind producing it.

It would be a mistake to replace the narrative of decline with an equally simple narrative of wisdom, in which age brings a serenity and judgement that compensate for everything else. Older people are not uniformly wise, and losses in speed and working memory have real consequences, for learning a new technology, for instance, or for following a fast conversation in a noisy room. The more defensible view is that ageing changes the mix of a person's capacities rather than lowering a single level, and that whether the change amounts to a loss depends on the task. In a setting that rewards speed with novel material, the young will usually have the advantage; in one that rewards the recognition of familiar patterns, a wide vocabulary or an accurate sense of how situations tend to unfold, the advantage may lie the other way. A good deal of everyday competence, from running a household to reading the mood of a tense meeting, belongs to the second kind. A society that judges older minds only by the first kind of task will find decline wherever it looks.

passage: Epicurus held that death is nothing to us, since where death is, we are not, and his Roman follower Lucretius added an argument that has been discussed ever since. Look back, Lucretius suggests, at the endless stretch of time that passed before you were born, which did not trouble you then and does not trouble you now. The time after your death is a mirror held up to that earlier time, and it would be inconsistent to dread the one while feeling nothing about the other. If non-existence before birth is no evil, non-existence after death can be none either.

The argument has a pleasing economy, and against one target it is decisive. Many people who fear death picture it, half consciously, as a condition they will find themselves in: a darkness, a silence, an interminable wait. Against this picture the mirror works admirably: nobody imagines that they spent the centuries before their birth sitting patiently in the dark, and the comparison exposes the fear of being dead as a confusion, since there will be no one there to suffer the darkness.

But most people who fear death are not chiefly afraid of a condition; they are afraid of losing what they would otherwise have had: the next conversation, the completion of their work, the sight of their children grown. Here the symmetry breaks down, because our attitudes to past and future are not symmetrical even in ordinary life; we look forward to pleasures and dread pains that are still to come in a way that has no counterpart for those already over. More importantly, the goods we stand to lose by dying are goods that this very life would have contained had it continued, whereas the goods of the centuries before our birth were never ours to lose. A person could hardly have been born a hundred years earlier and remained the same person, with the same parents and history; but the same person can very easily die later than he in fact does.

This does not mean that Lucretius has nothing to teach. If the fear of death is partly a fear of a condition, then his argument removes part of the fear, and that is no small gift. What remains is better described as grief in advance for a life cut short, and grief of that kind is not a confusion to be argued away. It is the shadow cast by caring about one's own future, and a consolation that worked perfectly against it would have to work by teaching us to care less.

passage: When a town loses its newspaper, the loss is usually mourned in the language of community: the obituaries, the school sports results, the notices of births and marriages that no one else will print. These are real losses, but they are not the ones that matter most for self-government. What disappears with the local paper is something duller and more important, namely the habit of attendance. For decades, in many places, a reporter sat through the meetings of the council, the planning committee and the school board, read the budget documents that nobody else read, and noticed when a contract went to the same firm for the third time without a tender.

Most of what such reporters wrote was unremarkable, and much of it was barely read. Its value lay less in any particular story than in the knowledge, shared by every official in the room, that someone was taking notes. Officials who know that a question may be asked in print tomorrow tend to ask it of themselves today. Monitoring of this kind works rather as a speed camera does: its effect is measured not by the fines it issues but by the careless driving it prevents. Remove it, and the immediate result is not a wave of scandal, since there is no longer anyone to report one, but a gradual loosening of the restraint that observation imposed. The absence of bad news, in a town without a reporter, is not evidence of good government.

It is often said that the internet has more than made up the difference, since anyone can now publish and residents can share information instantly. This confuses the supply of commentary with the supply of attention. A neighbourhood forum can spread a rumour about the council in minutes, but it seldom has anyone willing to spend three evenings a month in council meetings, or the training to read a set of accounts. National outlets, for their part, cover local government only when it produces a story large enough to interest a national audience, which is usually to say only after the damage is done. What the internet has multiplied is reaction; what has thinned out is the patient, unglamorous observation on which informed reaction depends.

None of this should be allowed to turn into nostalgia. Many local papers were timid with powerful advertisers, cosy with the town's leading figures and given to boosterism, celebrating every new development while asking few questions about who would profit from it. A press that depends on the goodwill of the people it covers is a weak watchdog, and some of the papers now lamented were weak in exactly this way, flattering the very people they ought to have been questioning. The case for local journalism does not rest on the virtue of the institutions that happened to provide it.

It rests, rather, on the function those institutions performed, however imperfectly. If that function is to survive the collapse of the business model that once paid for it, it will have to be supported deliberately: by newsrooms funded as public goods, by universities that send students to cover meetings, perhaps by public records published in forms that a busy citizen can actually read. Each of these options carries hazards, and money from the very governments that journalists are meant to watch carries the most obvious one. But a democracy that leaves the observation of its local governments to chance should not be surprised when those governments begin to behave as if no one is looking.

passage: An economy organised entirely by prices would have no need of firms. Every task, from sweeping a floor to designing a circuit, could be bought from whoever offered it most cheaply, and each worker would be a small business selling services by the hour. That actual economies look nothing like this is so familiar that it rarely seems to require explanation. Yet it does. Inside a firm, resources move not because a price has changed but because someone has been told to move them, and the coexistence of these two methods of coordination, the market outside and the hierarchy within, is one of the quieter puzzles of economic life.

The standard answer is that using the market is not free. Before anything can be bought, a buyer must find sellers, compare their terms, write a contract and then check that the contract has been honoured. When a task recurs daily and its details cannot be specified in advance, these costs multiply, and it becomes cheaper to hire someone on open-ended terms and direct the work as it arises. On this view the firm is a device for economising on bargaining: it grows until the cost of organising one more activity internally equals the cost of buying it outside. The account has real explanatory power. It predicts, correctly, that firms tend to bring in-house the activities that are specific to their own operations, where a supplier who knew it was indispensable could hold them to ransom.

What the account leaves out is suggested by its own vocabulary. It describes the firm almost entirely in terms of costs avoided, as if the best a firm could do were to match what an ideal market would have delivered at no expense. But a group of people who work together for years does not merely save on contracts; it produces something that no contract could have bought. Such a group learns which of its members can be trusted with ambiguity, how to divide a problem that none of them fully understands, and which shortcuts are safe. This knowledge is rarely written down and often cannot be, because it lives in habits and in the expectations people hold of one another. It cannot be purchased from outside because it does not exist outside; it is a product of the firm's continued existence.

None of this overturns the bargaining view, which remains the best guide to where the boundary of a firm will fall in any particular case. A carmaker deciding whether to make its own seats is weighing exactly the costs that view describes. The difficulty arises only when the account is taken as a complete theory of what firms are for. Then it makes the firm look like a regrettable necessity, a patch over the imperfections of exchange, and it renders the most valuable thing a firm possesses, the shared competence of people who have learned to work together, invisible to the very analysis that claims to explain it.

passage: Discussion of whether photographs can be trusted has long been dominated by the fear of manipulation. Early critics worried about staged scenes and retouched negatives; later ones about software that can add a figure to a crowd or remove one from a podium without leaving a trace visible to the eye. These worries are reasonable, and the tools that prompt them have become more powerful. But they direct attention to the least interesting way in which a photograph can mislead, and in doing so they leave the more ordinary and more pervasive problem almost untouched.

Consider an unaltered photograph of a crowded square taken during a demonstration. Every figure in it was really there, standing exactly where the picture shows. The image is, in the narrow sense, entirely truthful. Yet it cannot tell us whether the square was full or whether the photographer stood at the one corner where people had gathered; whether the moment captured was typical of the afternoon or its single tense minute; whether the raised fists at the front belonged to protesters or to the counter-demonstration across the road. A photograph is accurate about what falls inside its frame and wholly silent about what falls outside it, and the frame is chosen by someone.

This is why the manipulation debate can produce a false sense of security. A viewer who has learned to check for doctored pixels may conclude that an image which passes the check is reliable, when the check has said nothing about selection, timing or framing. An honest photograph can support a dishonest story as easily as a forged one can, and often more easily, since it will survive the very scrutiny that exposes a forgery.

None of this makes photographs worthless as evidence. It means that their evidential value lies less in the single image than in its surroundings: the caption that states when and where it was taken, the other frames from the same roll or memory card, the identity and record of the person who took it, the existence of independent pictures of the same event. A photograph considered alone is a fragment that can be fitted into many stories. A photograph considered with these supports begins to narrow the stories it can serve. The question to ask of an image, then, is not only whether it has been altered but what would have to be true of everything around it for it to mean what it is said to mean.

passage: Each new medium of reading arrives with a lament attached. The prevailing anxiety is that screens are making us worse readers: that a generation raised on phones can no longer follow a sustained argument, and that anything read on a device is necessarily read badly. Some of this anxiety is supported by evidence. A number of studies have reported that people tend to understand long and demanding texts somewhat less well on screens than on paper, especially when they are working against the clock. But the usual interpretation of such findings, that the screen itself damages comprehension, is too quick.

Consider what readers characteristically do on screens. Most of what they encounter there is brief, and much of it is read in order to decide whether to read it at all: headlines, messages, feeds, search results. Over years, this produces a thoroughly practised habit of skimming, in which the eye hunts for familiar key words and moves on, and when the same reader is later handed a dense essay on a tablet, the habit accompanies the device. The reader skims because skimming is what that screen has always been for, and comprehension suffers accordingly. On this account the difficulty lies less in the glass than in the expectations that the glass has gradually trained.

This explanation carries a more encouraging implication. Habits, unlike physiological limitations, can be changed, and some of the gaps reported in the research seem to narrow when readers are given more time, or are asked to slow down and summarise what they have read. A reader who approaches a screen with the deliberate intentions he would bring to a printed book may perform nearly as well as he would with the book itself. The underlying capacity for sustained attention is not lost; it is simply not being called upon.

Yet none of this shows that the medium makes no difference at all. Paper offers a reader a sense of place that a scrolling screen does not: the thickness of the pages already read, the position of a passage on the left or right page, the feel of a chapter's length in the hand. These cues help some readers remember where an idea appeared and how a long argument is organised, and a screen supplies them only weakly. The sensible conclusion is therefore a qualified one. Screens are not destroying our capacity to read deeply, but they make it easier not to, and readers and teachers who want deep reading on screens will have to ask for it deliberately rather than expect it by default.

passage: Each summer, the arrival of the monsoon over the southern tip of the Indian peninsula is announced on a particular day, and the date is reported as if something had been observed to happen: the rains have come. Newspapers compare it with the long-term average, and a delay of a week becomes a story about anxious farmers and rising food prices. Behind the announcement, however, lies not an event but a decision. The monsoon has no sharp leading edge. Showers build over days or weeks, winds shift gradually, and early bursts of rain may be followed by long dry spells. To fix a single day, forecasters must apply criteria, thresholds of rainfall across a set of stations and of wind and cloud, chosen so that the date can be determined consistently from one year to the next.

Calling the onset a convention is not to call it arbitrary. Good criteria pick out a real change in the behaviour of the atmosphere, and fixing them in advance prevents the date from being adjusted to suit hopes or headlines. A consistent definition also makes years comparable, so that researchers can ask whether onsets have tended to come earlier or later over many decades. Conventions of this kind are the ordinary machinery of science; the point at which a heavy shower counts as an extreme rainfall event, or a tropical storm as a cyclone, is fixed in the same way.

The trouble begins when the convention is mistaken for the thing it marks. A declared onset tells a farmer that a threshold was crossed somewhere along the coast; it does not tell her whether the soil in her own district holds enough moisture for seed to survive the next fortnight. In some years the rains, having satisfied the criteria, stall for weeks, and farmers who sowed on the strength of the announcement watch their seedlings wither. The date did nothing wrong; it was simply asked to answer a question it was never designed to answer.

The lesson is not that the onset date should be abolished, since it serves research and public communication reasonably well, but that a single number cannot serve every purpose at once. A measure built for comparing years across a century need not be the measure that should guide a decision about sowing next week. Agricultural advice would be better anchored in local indicators, such as accumulated rainfall and soil moisture in the district concerned, with the national date treated as background rather than as a signal to act. Definitions in climate science, like definitions elsewhere, should be judged by whether they fit the decision they are used to inform.

passage: Every wave of labour-saving machinery revives an old piece of arithmetic. If a factory needs a fixed quantity of work done, and a new machine does a third of it, then a third of the workers must go. Extend the sum across a whole economy and the conclusion seems inescapable: the more productive we become, the fewer of us will be needed. Economists have a name for the premise hidden in this calculation. They call it the lump of labour fallacy, the assumption that there is a set amount of work to be shared out, so that any work done by a machine, a newcomer or a pensioner who stays on is necessarily work taken from someone else.

The premise fails because the quantity of work is not fixed; it depends on what people want and can afford. When a machine makes cloth cheaper, households that once owned two shirts buy five, and the money they no longer spend on clothing goes on furniture, travel or schooling, each of which employs someone. The jobs created in this way are rarely the jobs that were lost, and they often appear in places and trades that nobody at the time thought to connect with the original invention. That is precisely why the destruction is so visible and the creation so easy to overlook. A closed mill is a single event with an address; the thousand small expansions that follow are scattered across an economy and are reported, if at all, as ordinary growth.

The same error appears in proposals that look generous. Schemes to push older workers into early retirement so that the young can find work, or to cap weekly hours so that employment is spread more thinly, assume that the jobs given up by one group pass intact to another. There is little reason to expect this. A worker who retires early also stops earning and spending at the old rate, and a firm that loses an experienced employee may simply produce less rather than hire a novice to take her place.

None of this means that the anxiety is foolish. The fallacy concerns the total amount of work, not its distribution, and a correct argument about totals is cold comfort to a fifty-year-old weaver whose skills no longer have a buyer. Transitions can take a generation, and the people who bear their cost are seldom the people who collect the gains. The proper conclusion is narrower than either side usually admits: technology does not abolish work in aggregate, but it can ruin particular lives and places, and policy ought to be judged by what it does for them rather than by whether it rescues a fixed stock of jobs that never existed.

passage: A long tradition in the philosophy of science treats explanation and prediction as two faces of one achievement. To explain why an event happened, on this view, is to show that it could have been expected, given the relevant laws and the conditions that held beforehand; to predict an event is to perform the same derivation before the event rather than after it. The symmetry is attractive because it makes explanation answerable to something. An explanation that could not, even in principle, have served as a prediction would seem to be no more than a story told after the fact. The view also promised a single standard for the whole of science, from astronomy, where eclipses are calculated centuries ahead, to clinical medicine, where a diagnosis is expected both to account for a patient's symptoms and to anticipate their course.

Yet the symmetry fails in both directions. A falling barometer reading is an excellent predictor of a coming storm, and anyone who knows the correlation can forecast the weather with it; but no one supposes that the barometer explains the storm. Both are effects of a drop in atmospheric pressure, and the reading earns its predictive power by riding on that common cause. Conversely, we can often explain what we could never have predicted. A geologist can say why a particular hillside gave way, pointing to saturated soil and a weakened layer of clay, without having been able to say beforehand that it would fail that week rather than in some other year. The explanation is sound even though the forecast was out of reach.

What these cases suggest is that explanation and prediction answer to different demands. A predictor need only be reliably connected with what it predicts; it does not matter how the connection arises. An explanation must identify what the outcome depends on: the factors such that, had they been different, the outcome would have been different too. The barometer fails that test, since a broken barometer would not have prevented the storm; the clay passes it, since firmer clay would have held the slope.

None of this makes prediction irrelevant to explanation. A claim about what an outcome depends on usually implies something about what would happen under other conditions, and checking those implications is how such claims are tested. A theory that explains everything and forbids nothing should make us suspicious. But the test is a check on an explanation, not its substance. To confuse the two is to mistake the evidence that an account is right for the thing that makes it an account at all.

passage: A respectable argument holds that negative criticism of new books is a waste of everyone's time. So many books are published each year that no critic can notice more than a sliver of them; the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious, and to spend it explaining why a book is bad is to deny it to a book that deserves attention. On this view the most damning verdict a critic can deliver is silence. A poor book left unmentioned simply sinks, and nothing is lost except the pleasure that some critics take in wounding. The position has the further appeal of seeming kind, which is no small recommendation in a literary world where writers and critics are often the same people.

The argument is tidy, but it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read. If that were so, the notice of a weak book would indeed be wasted, since a reader who is told merely to skip something has learned nothing that he could use elsewhere. But criticism has always done something besides sorting. A careful account of why a book fails is also an account of what success would have looked like, and in giving it the critic makes public a set of standards that readers can test, dispute and apply for themselves. The reader who follows a well-argued case against a novel he admired may end unconvinced, yet he will read the next novel more alertly.

There is a further cost to silence. If critics write only about the books they admire, praise becomes the sole currency of criticism, and like any currency issued without limit it loses its value. A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way. Readers soon learn to discount it, as they discount the admiring phrases printed on the cover of every new book, and the critic whose praise is sincere is then heard no more clearly than the publicist. The possibility of dispraise is what gives praise its meaning.

None of this licenses cruelty, and the case for restraint does have force in one kind of instance. A modest first novel from a small press, which few people will encounter anyway, gains nothing from a public demolition, and neither do its readers. The negative notice earns its space when the book in question is prominent: widely praised, heavily promoted, or likely to shape what others write. There the critic who dissents is not kicking someone who is down but contesting a reputation that is already shaping public taste, and that is among the most useful things criticism can do.
